The model assumes that the room heats up evenly with the valve open and cools towards the outside temperature with the valve closed. The more days with different weather, the more accurate it gets.

Once a day the app predicts from the active profile, the room model and the forecast when each heat-up will reach its target, and compares this with the measurement afterwards. Nothing is changed at the heating. Times with an open window or a manual change don\'t count.

Shows which circuit of your floor heating is open right now, records the history, learns how each room behaves and makes heating profiles easy to edit. Free, no ads, no tracking. Unofficial project, not affiliated with eQ-3.
If you like the app, a voluntary contribution is always appreciated. It is never required and doesn\'t unlock anything.

PureHeat reads your floor heating through the Homematic IP cloud and shows what the official app doesn\'t: which valve is open, how each room behaves over time and how it could be heated better.
Enter the SGTIN from the label underneath the access point (and the PIN if you set one). When asked, press the blue button on the access point. The access token is stored on this phone only.

One card per room: actual and target temperature, humidity and the opening of each valve (circuit). Towel radiators with a radiator thermostat appear as their own rooms without a temperature sensor. The overview refreshes every 5 minutes while the app is open; “Refresh” fetches immediately.

The system only knows how far a valve is open, not whether warm water actually flows. A stuck valve pin, a cold supply from the central heating or air in the circuit all look like “valve open”. If a valve is open for hours and the room doesn\'t get warmer, the app shows a warning – check the circuit at the manifold then.

The small chart shows the last 24 hours: actual temperature (line), target temperature (dashed), valve opening (area below) and humidity (own panel – percent and °C don\'t share a scale). Labels above the chart mark when a window was opened or closed and when the target changed (rounded to 15 minutes). Tap the chart or “History ›” for all data up to 60 days, with outside temperature, each channel and exact values at any time. The top of the overview shows the outside temperature and the forecast for the next 24 hours.

Without window contacts the app recognises an open window from the temperature: a quick drop while the valve is closed. A rise again without heating counts as “closed”. If the heating starts while the window may still be open, the app only says “at least until”. Detection works best with dense recordings (see “Battery”).

From the recorded phases the app learns per room how fast it loses heat (k), how strongly the floor heating heats it (P) and how long the screed takes to respond (dead time). From this it predicts how long the room needs from setback to comfort temperature and back at the current outside temperature. Open-window times are left out. Until enough phases have been seen, it shows “still learning”.

Before the app may ever control the heating, it has to prove that its predictions are right. Once a day it predicts for each room when the next heat-ups of the active profile will reach their target, and checks this against the measurement afterwards. The detail view shows the hit rate. Only after 14 days with at least 80 % on time is an optimal control offered – and you switch it on yourself.

Under “Describe room ›” in the history of a room you describe it in your own words, typed or dictated – e.g. size, ceiling height, how many windows face which direction, glazing, exterior walls, top floor or above a cellar, floor covering, roller shutters, a stove, use as bedroom, window tilted at night. On devices with on-device AI (Gemini Nano) the app recognises the properties with it, otherwise by keywords; you check and correct the result before saving. Until the room model has learned from the history, these properties set its starting values (e.g. carpet heats more slowly, an attic room loses heat faster). Later, south windows will help to account for sunshine.

“Heating profile ›” shows the weekly profiles of a room. Tap a day to edit it: drag the edges of the phases, set start, end and temperature precisely, copy a day to others. Before saving, the app lists every change, backs up the old version, saves and then reads the profile back to check it. “Undo last save” restores the backup. Nothing is written without your confirmation.

In the background the app fetches every 15 minutes while something is changing, otherwise every 30 minutes and every 60 minutes at night. Each fetch is about 100 KB. Android may delay these jobs for hours if the app is rarely opened – for a complete history set App info → Battery → “Unrestricted”.
The app follows the system language. You can choose another language under “Info” or (Android 13+) in the system settings under “App languages”.

The app talks to the Homematic IP cloud and, for the weather forecast, to Open-Meteo (free, no account). Open-Meteo only receives the location of the home rounded to about 1 km, a few times a day. Access data and history stay on this phone. PureHeat is an unofficial project and not affiliated with eQ-3.
The new name is saved in the Homematic IP cloud and also shows up in the official app.

Nothing detected in this period. Detected is a quick rise in humidity while the temperature doesn\'t fall.
Detected from a quick rise in humidity. The room model leaves these times out: the hot water heats the room, not the floor heating.

For rooms described as bathroom or with a shower or bathtub, the app recognises showering and bathing from a quick rise in humidity (at least 5 percentage points within minutes) while the temperature doesn\'t fall. The times are marked in the charts and listed in the room view. The room model leaves them out, because the hot water heats the room, not the floor heating. By default, thermostats whose name contains a room\'s name (e.g. a towel radiator) appear right after that room; “Order” on the overview lets you arrange the rooms yourself.

Under “Info” → “Data” you can export all measurements (as CSV tables, readable in spreadsheets or for analyses) together with your settings as one ZIP file: “Export and share” opens the Android share sheet (e.g. Google Drive, mail), “Save as file” lets you pick a folder, including Google Drive. “Import” reads such a file, e.g. on a new phone: measurements are added, settings replaced. The export contains room names but no access data – after a move to a new phone you connect the access point again.

Write or dictate when it should be how warm, e.g. “Weekdays 6–8 and 17–22 at 21 °C, weekend 8–23 at 21 °C, otherwise 17 °C”. The app fills the week below as a suggestion – nothing is saved until you check it and tap “Save”.

In the heating profile screen, “Create from description” lets you write or dictate the week in your own words, e.g. “Weekdays 6–8 and 17–22 at 21 °C, weekend 8–23, otherwise 17 °C”. The on-device AI (without it: keyword recognition for English and German) turns it into heating phases; days you don\'t mention stay as they are. The suggestion appears in the week view – check it, adjust it if needed and save as usual, with the list of changes and the backup.
No access point at hand? The demo shows a sample flat with invented data – nothing is sent anywhere. Tap “Log out” to leave it.
